newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Paris stocks end with gains despite Left win.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Paris stocks end with gains despite Left win.

text.p: Paris stocks ended with healthy gains after a day of roller-coaster trading with investors trying to second-guess the impact of the new Socialist-led government on business.
In currencies, the dollar was up two pfennigs against the mark in late dealings as the shock left-wing victory in the French parliamentary elections sent players scurrying into safe-haven currencies.

Elsewhere in Europe, Frankfurt stocks closed up nearly two percent with the export sector boosted by the stronger dollar but London shares finished well down, unsettled by fresh worries over interest rates.

But it was the French markets that held most attention. The Paris bourse swung from minus three percent to plus two percent as investors initially took fright at the left's victory, then decided to give them the benefit of the doubt.

The blue-chip CAC-40 index plummeted 85.19 points to 2,498.75 within minutes of the opening as markets digested a "worst case scenario" for French markets in which the Socialist-led left would need the Communists to form a government.
But the market recovered its nerve and was up to 2,645.86 by midafternoon in heavy trading. Some of the gaiins were later eroded but the index was still up a respectable 0.68 percent at the close.
Sentiment changed as investors came round to the view that the incoming Socialists would not adopt market-unfriendly policies.

"People aren't that scared," one trader said. "They can't raise taxes. The right already did that. They can make life miserable for companies trying to restructure but they can't stop that. They'll do symbolic things."

"Everyone was worried the Americans would sell but when they didn't sell in any big volume, the market rose. Then everyone thought the rise was overdone for the day after an election so there has been some consolidation," said one dealer.
Best performers were consumer stocks and those with international exposure, while investors were selling privatisation shares, particularly in the defence sector and financial sector.

In Frankfurt, bourse floor trade finished with gains of 1.6 percent, shaking off worries about the future of Europe's currency union and a row between the German government and the Bundesbank about revaluing assets.
In after-hours trading on the computerised IBIS index, stocks climbed, helped partly by the stronger dollar, which improved prospects for exporters, particularly the chemicals sector.
"Germany should have been down a lot today, because of the French election and doubts about the euro, but instead it's rallying. A lot is coming from the dollar," a German share trader said.

In contrast, London ended the day down 1.27 percent, one of the biggest one-day declines for two months as bank stocks tumbled and fears grew of a possible rise in British interest rates later this week.
Worries over the Labour government's first budget, confirmed for July 2, also helped send the FTSE index 58.5 points lower at 4,562.8 -- its biggest fall since a 65-point loss on April 1.
With Wall Street unsettled by fresh fears of a rise in interest rates, the London market was in a gloomy mood, setting the scene for what analysts and traders said could be a jittery month.
The long-awaited market debut of banking group Halifax dominated trading activity, prompting profit-taking in other financial stocks as investment funds cashed in gains in the sector.
In currency markets, the dollar could do no wrong amid renewed uncertainty about the single European currency.

As Socialist Lionel Jospin became France's new prime minister, the market was hit by fears the left's election victory would mean a broadly based, weak euro currency or a delay in economic and monetary union.

The dollar was trading at 1.7265 marks, two pfennigs up from late Friday's European level of 1.7075. It earlier touched 1.7310 marks, its strongest rate since May 6. Against the French franc, it jumped to near one-month peaks of 5.8302, compared to 5.7705 on Friday

With the French Socialists needing the Communists to form a government and pledging a Europe without austerity, analysts said the market was now fretting that this meant either delay or a broad-based, soft euro.
"Neither of those will be palatable to the European bloc -- near-term it seems the dollar is the winner," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International.

Fears of a broad, weak European single currency were fuelled by French Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande, who called for Italy and Spain to be included in EMU and said all stood to benefit if the euro "no longer means austerity".
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted at 1.7265 marks and 116.57 yen, compared with 1.7075 marks and 116. 37 yen in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed down 58.5 points at 4,562.8
PARIS - The CAC-40 ended up 17.51 points at 2,601.45 FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed up 57.78 points at 3605.62.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $344.05 an ounce, compared to Friday's close of $344.65. Silver was unchanged at $4.74 in late trading.
